citation.title: Randomization-based confidence sets for the local average treatment effect

standing_assumptions: [Units, potential outcomes, compliance: main p. 3 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.1] We consider an experiment with $n$ units, where each unit is randomized to treatment or control. Let $y_i(d, z)$ denote the potential outcome of unit $i$ under the potential compliance decision $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and the treatment assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$. Let $d_i(z)$ denote the compliance decision of the $i$th unit when under treatment status $z$. We write $d_i(1) = 0$ if the $i$th unit is assigned to treatment, but does not receive treatment, and write $d_i(1) = 1$ if it does. The compliance decision $d_i(0)$ under assignment to control is defined analogously. [...] Let $[n] = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Assumption 1 (Exclusion restriction). For all $i \in [n]$, $y_i(d, z)$ is independent of $z$. This assumption implies that treatment assignment affects outcomes only through treatment receipt, and hence $y_i(d, 1) = y_i(d, 0)$ for all $i \in [n]$. Given this assumption, we write $y_i(d)$ from now on to denote the potential outcome under treatment status $d$. [main p. 4 (PDF p. 4)] Assumption 2 (Monotonicity). For all $i \in [n]$, we have $d_i(1) \ge d_i(0)$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the set of compliers, $\mathcal{C} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0,\ d_i(1) = 1\}$. (1) Our inferential target is the LATE in the experimental sample, defined by $\bar\beta = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{y_i(1) - y_i(0)\}$. (2) We assume throughout the paper that there is at least one complier ($|\mathcal{C}| \ge 1$) so that the quantity is well-defined. [Design and data: main p. 4, Section 2.2] We assume that the experiments under consideration are completely randomized: among $n$ units, researchers assign $n_1$ units to treatment, chosen uniformly at random. [...] For each unit $i$, we let $Z_i$ be a random variable such that $Z_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is assigned to treatment and $Z_i = 0$ otherwise. By definition, $\mathrm{pr}(Z_i = 1) = n_1/n$, and we introduce the shorthand $\pi = n_1/n$. For each unit $i$, researchers observe compliance decisions $D_i = d_i(Z_i)$ and outcomes $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$. Each unit $i$ may additionally be associated with some covariate information [...]; if so, this information is collected in a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$. Throughout the paper we assume that $k$ does not change with the sample size $n$. [...] We adopt the finite-population (design-based) framework, treating the potential outcomes and compliance decisions as fixed parameters [...]. The sole source of randomness in our model is the vector of random treatment assignments, and statistical uncertainties are evaluated exclusively with respect to this randomness. [Studentized statistic: main pp. 4-5, Section 3.1] For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, we define the statistic $\hat\tau(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i - \pi)$. [...] A short calculation shows that $\hat\tau(\beta) = \pi(1-\pi)\left\{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}$, where $n_0 = n - n_1$ [...]. We further define $\hat v_i(1, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^n Z_j(Y_j - \beta D_j)$, $\hat v_i(0, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{j=1}^n (1 - Z_j)(Y_j - \beta D_j)$. (3) Using this notation, we define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat v_i^2(1, \beta) + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat v_i^2(0, \beta)$ and the studentized statistic $\Delta(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau(\beta)}{\hat\sigma(\beta)}$. (4) We will use the absolute value $|\Delta(\beta)|$ as our test statistic and construct confidence sets by test inversion. We refer to the test statistic $\Delta(\beta)$ in (4) as the AR statistic. [Randomization distribution and confidence set: main pp. 5-6, Section 3.2] The assignment vector $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$ is a random vector in $\{0, 1\}^n$. Let $Z^*$ be a random vector with the same distribution as $Z$ and which is independent of $Z$. We use $\mathbb{P}^*$ to denote the conditional (on $Z$) probability measure induced by $Z^*$. We define $\hat\tau^* : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\hat\tau^*(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i^* - \pi)$, where we recall that by definition $Y_i$ and $D_i$ depend only on $Z_i$ and not on $Z_i^*$. We also define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2 + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2$ [the inner sums are the reassigned-arm means; the paper reuses the index $i$] and the studentized statistic $\Delta^*(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*(\beta)}$. (5) The distribution of $|\Delta^*(\beta)|$ under $\mathbb{P}^*$ is discrete and supported on $[0, \infty]$. For every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. (6) Our confidence set is defined as $I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (7) [Assumptions 3 and 4, parameter space $\Theta_n$: main pp. 6-8] Assumption 3 (Parameter space). Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $A > 0$ be given. Set $w_i(1) = y_i\{d_i(1)\} - \bar\beta d_i(1)$, $w_i(0) = y_i\{d_i(0)\} - \bar\beta d_i(0)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes and compliance decisions hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} \ge -\delta\,\sigma_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\,\sigma_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$. Here, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ is the complier-group covariance of adjusted potential outcomes, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(1) - \mu_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\}\{w_i(0) - \mu_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}\}$, where $\mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} w_i(a)$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$, and $\sigma^2_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}$ and $\sigma^2_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ are the complier-group potential outcome variances, $\sigma^2_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}}\}^2$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$. If $|\mathcal{C}| = 1$, all variances and covariances are defined to be zero. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $A$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}|^4\right\}^{1/4} \le A\sigma_{w(a)}$, where $\mu_{w(a)} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(a)$ and $\sigma^2_{w(a)} = (n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}\}^2$. [...] Assumption 4 (Completely randomized experiment). Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a constant $0 < r \le 1/2$, we have $n_1 \in [rn, (1-r)n]$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1-4 with $n$ units and constants $\delta$, $r$ and $A$ by $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$, where $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 3 with constants $\delta$ and $A$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. Each combination of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and an experimental design completely determines the distribution of our test statistic. [...] For each parameter $\theta$ in the parameter space, we denote its LATE by $\bar\beta(\theta)$. [Regression adjustment: main pp. 8-10, Sections 4.1-4.3] [...] each unit $i$ comes equipped with a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ of covariates for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We suppose that each $x_i$ is demeaned, meaning that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$, where $0_k$ denotes the zero vector in $\mathbb{R}^k$. [...] We denote the $s$th element of $x_i$ by $x_{si}$. Given a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a treatment assignment vector $Z$, consider the linear regression $Y_i - \beta D_i \sim (1 - Z_i)\varphi_0 + Z_i\varphi_1 + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_0 + Z_i x_i'\gamma_1$. (8) This is an interacted linear regression that regresses $Y_i - \beta D_i$ on $((1 - Z_i), Z_i, (1 - Z_i)x_i, Z_i x_i)$ without an intercept. For each $\beta$, denote the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimators resulting from (8) by $\hat\varphi(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$, corresponding to the order in which the associated coefficients appear in (8). We define the randomization statistics $\hat\varphi^*(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi^*(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma^*(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ similarly by using $Z^*$ instead of $Z$. [main p. 9] We define the covariate-adjusted difference-in-means statistic as $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(1, \beta)\} - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(0, \beta)\}$, (9) and we define the covariate-adjusted randomization estimator $\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ analogously, again replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$ and replacing $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$ by their randomization analogues. [...] The residual estimators associated with (8) and their randomization-based counterparts are $\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi(Z_i, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma(Z_i, \beta)$, $\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi^*(Z_i^*, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma^*(Z_i^*, \beta)$. We use these to define the variance estimators $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2$, $\hat\sigma^{2*}_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. The adjusted studentized difference-in-means statistics are then $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$, $\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$. (10) [...] Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. [main p. 10] Our proposed confidence set is $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (11) [Assumption 5 and parameter space $\Xi_n$: main pp. 10-11] Assumption 5. Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $\tilde\varepsilon, A, B > 0$ be given. For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\varepsilon_i(a, \bar\beta) = y_i\{d_i(a)\} - \bar\beta d_i(a) - \varphi(a, \bar\beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \bar\beta)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes, compliance decisions and covariates hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta),\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)} \ge -\delta\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta)}\sigma_{\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)}$. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $B$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^4(a, \bar\beta)\right\}^{1/4} \le B\sigma_{\varepsilon(a,\bar\beta)}$. (iii) We have that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$. (iv) For all $s \in [k]$ and the given $A$, we have that $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{si}^4 \le A$. (v) Let $\lambda_{\min}$ denote the smallest eigenvalue of $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i'$. Then for the given $\tilde\varepsilon$, $\lambda_{\min} \ge \tilde\varepsilon$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions, covariates and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 with $n$ units, covariates of dimension $k$, and constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$, $B$ and $r$ by $\Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$. Here, $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 5 with constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$ and $B$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. [The population variances and covariance in Assumption 5 are those of Supplement A.1 below, with divisor $n - 1$; $\varphi(a, \beta)$, $\gamma(a, \beta)$ are defined in Supplement D.2 below.] [Supplement A, notation: Supplement p. 21 (Supplement PDF p. 1)] We let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the positive integers [...]. We use the notation $\lesssim$ to denote inequalities that hold up to a constant independent of $n$. [...] We also define a set $\mathcal{A}$ of always-takers and a set $\mathcal{N}$ of never-takers by $\mathcal{A} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 1, d_i(1) = 1\}$, $\mathcal{N} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0, d_i(1) = 0\}$. Let $\mathcal{T}(1), \mathcal{T}(0) \subset [n]$ denote the sets of subjects in the treatment and control groups defined by $Z$, respectively, so that $\mathcal{T}(1) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 1\}$, $\mathcal{T}(0) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 0\}$. Given a vector $v$, we use $\|v\|_2$ to denote the standard $l_2$ vector norm. [...] A.1. For any vector $q = (q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population mean and variance by $\mu_q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i$, $\sigma_q^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)^2$. We also define within-group variances for each group $G \in \{\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{N}\}$ by $\sigma^2_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})^2$, where $\mu_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{i \in G} q_i$ if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. Given an additional vector $\tilde q = (\tilde q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population covariance by $\sigma_{q\tilde q} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q})$, and the within-group covariances by $\sigma_{q\tilde q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q,G})$, if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. A.2. Let $\mathcal{Z}$ be a mean zero, variance one normal random variable. [...] For an $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, define $z_{1-\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$ as the value such that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{Z} > z_{1-\alpha}) = \alpha$. [Supplement B.1 and B.3: Supplement p. 22 (PDF p. 2)] Lemma 2. For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, the variance of $\hat\tau(\beta)$ is $\operatorname{var}(\hat\tau(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{S_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (B.1) where $S_1^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(1, \beta)^2$, $S_0^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(0, \beta)^2$, $S_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (v_i(1, \beta) - v_i(0, \beta))^2$, (B.2) $v_i(1, \beta) = y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1))$, (B.3) $v_i(0, \beta) = y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0))$. (B.4) [...] Lemma 3. We have $E[\hat\tau(\beta)] = 0$ when $\beta = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}(y_i(1) - y_i(0))$. [Supplement C, conventions: Supplement p. 23 (PDF p. 3)] Throughout this section, we let $\delta, r, A$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 1, and set $\Theta_n = \Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$. The notation $\Theta_n$ encodes Assumptions 1-4. We typically denote elements of $\Theta_n$ by $\theta_n$. For each model $\theta_n$, we denote its local average treatment effect by $\bar\beta(\theta_n)$ [...]. In various lemmas below, we will consider subsequences $(\theta_{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of a given sequence $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ of models. We let $n_{1k}$ denote the number of elements in the treatment group of $\theta_{n_k}$, and $n_{0k}$ the number of elements in the control group of $\theta_{n_k}$, so that $n_{0k} + n_{1k} = n_k$. [...] For the remainder of the proofs, we will implicitly assume that the variances $\sigma^2_{w(a)}$, for $a \in \{0, 1\}$ as defined in Assumption 3, are both strictly positive. This entails no loss of generality provided we adopt the convention that $0/0 = 0$. If both variances are zero, then the complier treatment effect is constant and additive, so the exact coverage result of the randomization-based CI in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005) applies. [...] Similar comments apply to the proofs in Section D. [...] In results on sequences $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$, we will generally omit the $n$-dependence on $w_i(1)$, $w_i(0)$, and other model-dependent quantities for brevity. [Supplement C.3: Supplement pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 7-8)] We write $E^*$ and $\operatorname{var}^*$ for expectation and variance under the probability measure $\mathbb{P}^*$. By Lemma 3, for any $\beta$ we have $E^*[\hat\tau^*(\beta)] = 0$, and by Lemma 2, $\operatorname{var}^*(\hat\tau^*(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^{*2}(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^{*2}(\beta)}{n_0}$, (C.25) where $S_1^{*2}(\beta) = S_0^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)\right)^2$. (C.26) [...] We recall that $\mu_Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$, $\mu_D = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n D_i$ and define $\hat\mu_{y(d(a))} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} y_i(d_i(a))$, $\hat\mu_{d(a)} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} d_i(a)$, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$. [Supplement D, least-squares parameters and infeasible estimator: Supplement pp. 31-32 (PDF pp. 11-12)] We let $k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 2, and set $\Xi_n = \Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r)$. D.2. Suppose a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ is given. Then we define, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, outcomes $w_i(a, \beta)$ by $w_i(a, \beta) = y_i(d_i(a)) - \beta d_i(a)$. (D.1) We define the least-squares regression parameters $\varphi(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\gamma(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^k$, by $(\varphi(a, \beta), \gamma(a, \beta)) = \arg\min_{(s,t) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^k}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (w_i(a, \beta) - s - x_i't)^2$, (D.2) where we interpret $t$ as a column vector. We define the residuals for (D.2) by $\varepsilon_i(a, \beta) = w_i(a, \beta) - \varphi(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \beta)$. The parameters $\varphi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(a, \beta)$ are defined similarly, by replacing $w_i(a, \beta)$ with $Y_i - \beta D_i$ in (D.2), and we define the associated residuals $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)$ by $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \varphi^*(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma^*(a, \beta)$. (D.3) These definitions imply that $\varphi^*(0, \beta) = \varphi^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta) = \gamma^*(1, \beta)$. D.3. To analyze the asymptotic behavior of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$, we define the infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(1, \beta)) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(0, \beta))$. (D.4) The infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ is defined similarly, replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$, and $\gamma(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma(0, \beta)$ by $\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta)$, respectively. A straightforward adaptation of Lemma 2 shows that $\operatorname{var}(\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (D.5) where $\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(1, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(0, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon_i(1, \beta) - \varepsilon_i(0, \beta))^2$. Similarly, $\operatorname{var}^*(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta)}{n_0}$, $\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta) = \mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. (D.6) [Supplement E.1: Supplement p. 32 (PDF p. 12)] Denote $x_i^\circ = [0, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$ and $\tilde x_i = [1, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$. For $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$, $\hat\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\hat\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \hat\gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$. (E.1) We denote their randomization counterparts as $\psi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\hat\psi^*(a, \beta)$. Lemma 14. The following claims hold. 1. Theorem 7. Fix $k\in\mathbb N$ with $k\ge1$, $\delta\in\mathbb R$ with $\delta<1$, $\tilde\varepsilon,A,B>0$ and $r\in(0,1/2]$, and let $\Xi_n=\Xi_n(k,\delta,\tilde\varepsilon,A,B,r)$. For every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
\[
\lim_{\kappa\to0^+}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\beta\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\{\theta\in\Xi_n:\,\bar\beta(\theta)=\beta\}}\mathbb P_\theta\left(\left|\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)\right|>z_{1-\alpha/2}-\kappa\right)\le\alpha.
\qquad\text{(E.36, corrected)}
\]
The population-size index $n$ runs over all positive integers, and each supremum over an empty model class is $0$. The ordinary outer right-hand limit is asserted to exist in $[0,1]$; no ordinary inner sample-size limit is asserted. Relative to the printed display, the parameter space is changed from $\Theta_n$ to $\Xi_n$ and the inner limit is changed to a limit superior.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions: $\Xi_n=\Xi_n(k,\delta,\tilde\varepsilon,A,B,r)$ is the regression-adjusted parameter space of Theorem 2 (main p. 11; Supplement p. 31, Section D.1), satisfying Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5, with $k\ge1$, $\delta<1$, $\tilde\varepsilon,A,B>0$ and $0<r\le1/2$ fixed independently of $n,\beta,\kappa$; $\bar\beta(\theta)$ is the LATE of model $\theta$. The statistic is $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)=\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)/\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ from (10) (main p. 9), with $\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}$ the nonnegative square root of the adjusted residual-sum-of-squares variance estimator. Its absolute value is defined in $[0,\infty]$: ordinary absolute studentization at positive scale, $0$ when numerator and scale are both $0$, and $+\infty$ when the numerator is nonzero and the scale is $0$. On a rank-deficient arm, use one fixed measurable choice of a least-squares minimizer, agreeing with the unique normal-equations solution on full-rank arms. $\mathbb P_\theta$ is the exact probability over complete randomization. $\mathcal Z\sim N(0,1)$, $\Phi$ is its distribution function, and $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is the unique real number with $\mathbb P(\mathcal Z>z_{1-\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$ (Supplement p. 21). Define $T_n(\kappa)$ by the two suprema displayed in the statement, taking every empty supremum of probabilities in $[0,1]$ to be $0$. A negative cutoff gives probability $1$ for each existing model; at a zero cutoff the event remains the strict event $|\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}|>0$. Put $L(\kappa)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}T_n(\kappa)$. The outer limit means ordinary convergence of $L(\kappa)$ through positive real $\kappa\to0$, including existence of that limit. No positive population residual-variance condition is added to this theorem. Auxiliary normalized identities in the proof are used on their positive-denominator domains; zero population residual variance is handled separately. As printed, Supplement p. 39 (PDF p. 19), (E.36) has $\Theta_n$ under the inner supremum and an ordinary inner limit; its omitted proof refers to Lemma 17 and Theorem 6.

canonical_claim.note:
Both repairs are explicit: $\Theta_n$ is replaced by $\Xi_n$, as required for the regression-adjusted statistic, and the ordinary inner limit is replaced by $\limsup_{n\to\infty}$. The ordinary outer right-hand limit is preserved. This aligns the canonical claim with the supplied llm-audit description, the current text of P002-E013 and AronowAudit.P002.Wave1.corrected_theorem7_limsup. It does not merely assume existence of the ordinary inner limits or restrict the size index to feasible sizes.

Counterexample to the old inner-limit assertion: fix $(k,\delta,\tilde\varepsilon,A,B,r,\alpha)=(1,0,1,1,1,1/2,1/2)$. The two balance inequalities require $2n_1=n$, so $\Xi_n$ is empty at every odd $n$ and $T_n(\kappa)=0$ there. At $n=4m$, take $m$ copies of each pair $(x_i,u_i)\in\{-1,1\}^2$, set $y_i(0)=y_i(1)=u_i$, make every unit a complier, and take $n_1=2m$. Then $\bar\beta=0$, the population OLS coefficients are zero, the residuals equal $u$, the covariate second and fourth moments and the residual fourth moment equal $1$, and the residual variance is $n/(n-1)$. Thus these populations belong to the fixed Xi class, and their oracle and conservative variances both equal $4/(n-1)>0$.

For completeness, the actual adjusted statistic, rather than just an oracle upper bound, has a normal limit in this example. Write $a,b,c,d$ for the treatment counts in cells $(-1,-1),(-1,1),(1,-1),(1,1)$, and set $v_-=a+b$, $v_+=c+d$, so $v_-+v_+=2m$. Outside the two assignments with a singular arm, the feasible adjusted numerator is $(b+d-m)(1/v_-+1/v_+)$, its oracle counterpart is $2(b+d-m)/m$, and the sum of the two arm residual sums of squares is $4m-\{(b-a)^2+(d-c)^2\}(1/v_-+1/v_+)$. Complete randomization gives $v_-/m\to1$, $v_+/m\to1$ and $a,b,c,d=m/2+O_{\mathbb P}(\sqrt m)$; the probability of the two singular assignments is $2/\binom{4m}{2m}\to0$. Consequently the feasible numerator equals its oracle counterpart times a factor tending to $1$ in probability, and $\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{adj}}/[4/(4m-1)]\to1$ in probability. The treated positive-response count $b+d$ is hypergeometric with mean $m$ and variance $m^2/(4m-1)$, so the finite-population CLT and Slutsky give $|\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(0)|\Rightarrow|\mathcal Z|$. For $q=z_{3/4}$ and every $0<\kappa<q$, the tail at $q-\kappa$ therefore tends to $2\{1-\Phi(q-\kappa)\}>1/2$ along $n=4m$. This is a lower bound on the model supremum along that subsequence, incompatible with the odd-size zeros. Failure occurs for every such $\kappa$, arbitrarily close to zero.

Check of the repair: the oracle CLT, numerator approximation and conservative variance-estimator bounds give, for each $t>0$, a uniform upper bound $\limsup_n\sup_{\beta}\sup_{\theta\in\Xi_n:\bar\beta(\theta)=\beta}\mathbb P_\theta(|\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)|>t)\le\mathbb P(|\mathcal Z|>t)$. The zero-residual models are included by a separate degeneracy argument, not a new positivity hypothesis. For $0<\kappa<z_{1-\alpha/2}$ apply this bound at $t=z_{1-\alpha/2}-\kappa$ and use continuity of the normal tail. Also $L(\kappa)=\limsup_n T_n(\kappa)$ is nondecreasing in $\kappa$ and lies in $[0,1]$, so its ordinary right-hand limit at zero exists and is at most $\alpha$. The unconditional Lean declaration corrected_theorem7_limsup proves precisely this conclusion without sorryAx; the archived corrected_theorem7 asserts the false ordinary inner limit and contains sorryAx. scratch/ClaimChecks.lean proves odd-size Xi emptiness and the zero supremum and checks these axiom dependencies. scratch/check_counterexamples.py enumerates the four-cell assignment counts with exact rational arithmetic; its full-rank rejection lower bounds do not depend on a singular-fit selection. The asymptotic counterexample argument here is a proof sketch; the architect's T21_assembly still takes three leaf propositions as hypotheses and is not claimed here as an unconditional Lean proof of that counterexample.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Finite-sample validity of the confidence sets (7) and (11) under a constant additive treatment effect (Sections 3.3 and 4.4; no numbered result)
canonical_claim.location: Main p. 6 (PDF p. 6), Section 3.3, first sentence; main p. 10 (PDF p. 10), Section 4.4, first sentence; also main pp. 4-5 (Section 3.1), p. 7 (Remark 2) and Supplement p. 23 (Supplement PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, main p. 6, Section 3.3] As noted in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005), the confidence set (7) is a finite-sample valid $(1 - \alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence set under a constant-additive-effect assumption. [As printed, main p. 10, Section 4.4] A straightforward extension of the reasoning in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005) shows that the confidence sets $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ are finite-sample valid if the constant-additive-effect condition holds, regardless of the value of $n$. [The reasoning, as printed, main pp. 4-5, Section 3.1] [Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005)] showed that, under a constant-additive-effect assumption and when $\beta$ is the true treatment effect, $Y_i - \beta D_i$ recovers the control outcomes $y_i(0)$ and is independent of the treatment assignments. Based on this observation, they used this statistic to construct randomization-based, finite-sample exact confidence sets under the constant-additive-effect assumption. [The constant-additive-effect assumption, as printed, main p. 7, Remark 2] When the potential outcomes obey the constant-additive-effect assumption (i.e., $y_i(1) = y_i(0) + \beta$ for all units $i$) [...]. [Formal content] Let $n \ge 2$, $1 \le n_1 \le n - 1$, and let the potential outcomes and compliance decisions satisfy Assumptions 1 and 2, with at least one complier, and $y_i(1) = y_i(0) + \beta$ for all $i \in [n]$ and some $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ (so that $\bar\beta = \beta$). Let $Z$ be completely randomized with $n_1$ treated units. Then (a) for every assignment, $Y_i - \beta D_i = y_i(0)$ for all $i$; (b) for every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\mathbb{P}\{\beta \in I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$; (c) with covariates $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$, for every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\mathbb{P}\{\beta \in I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions: Assumptions 1-2, compliers and $\bar\beta$ (main pp. 3-4); complete randomization, $D_i = d_i(Z_i)$, $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$ (main p. 4); $\Delta(\beta)$ (4), $\Delta^*(\beta)$ (5), $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$, the smallest (possibly infinite) value with $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$ (6), and $I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$ (7) (main pp. 4-6); $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}$, $\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}$ (10), $\eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}$ and $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ (11) (main pp. 8-10). $Z^*$ has the distribution of $Z$ and is independent of it; $\mathbb{P}^*$ is its law given $Z$; $\mathbb{P}$ is the law of $Z$. Conventions: $|\Delta^*(\beta)|$ takes values in $[0, \infty]$ (main p. 6) and $0/0 = 0$ (Supplement p. 23). [Supplement p. 23 (PDF p. 3), the same claim used in the proofs] If both variances are zero, then the complier treatment effect is constant and additive, so the exact coverage result of the randomization-based CI in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005) applies.
canonical_claim.note: The paper states this in prose, citing Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005); it has no numbered statement or proof, so the formal content was written here from the printed sentences. 'Finite-sample valid' is formalized as coverage at least $1 - \alpha$ at every $n$: with the non-strict acceptance rule of (7) and a discrete randomization distribution, coverage can exceed $1 - \alpha$ (the readers computed 0.943, 0.905, 0.968 at nominal 0.90, 0.90, 0.95 for $n = 8, 9, 10$), and under P002-T4 it can equal 1. Proof idea: by (a) the vector $(Y_i - \beta D_i)_i$ is the same for every assignment, so $|\Delta(\beta)|$ is a fixed function $g$ of $Z$ and $|\Delta^*(\beta)|$ is the same function of $Z^*$; $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ is then the non-random $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of $g(Z^*)$, and $\mathbb{P}\{g(Z) \le \eta\} = \mathbb{P}^*\{g(Z^*) \le \eta\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. The statement concerns the sets (7) and (11) built from the full randomization distribution, not the Monte Carlo sets (13)-(14). For (c) the paper does not say how the arm regressions are defined when an arm's design matrix is rank-deficient; the argument goes through for any rule that depends only on the adjusted outcomes, the covariates and the assignment (state the rule chosen). Remark 5's extension to multiple treatment levels is not part of this target.
